title: MCP 2026-07-28 Spec: Stateless Core, Apps, and Enterprise Auth
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol shipped its largest specification revision since launch. The `2026-07-28` release moves MCP from a mostly stateful, single-connection protocol to a stateless core built to scale on ordinary HTTP infrastructure, and adds an Extensions framework that several major features now build on. This page covers what changed and why it matters for anyone running MCP servers in production.

---

## Stateless Protocol Core

Earlier MCP transports (stdio, then HTTP/SSE) generally assumed a long-lived session pinned to one server instance — fine for a local process, awkward for a server running behind a load balancer. The 2026-07-28 spec restructures the core protocol so a client's requests no longer require sticky sessions or server-held state between calls.

**Practical effect:** servers can now scale horizontally behind a simple round-robin load balancer. Operators no longer need to implement sticky sessions or a shared session store just to run more than one server replica.

---

## Extensions Framework

The spec formalizes an **Extensions** mechanism — a way to add optional capabilities to MCP without bloating the core protocol or breaking clients that don't support them. Two extensions shipped alongside the core spec:

### MCP Apps
Lets a server ship an interactive HTML interface alongside a tool, rendered by the host in a sandboxed iframe. Tools declare their UI templates ahead of time, so a host can prefetch, cache, and security-review the UI before any code runs. The rendered UI communicates back to the host over the same JSON-RPC base protocol used for everything else in MCP — there's no separate side-channel to secure.

### Tasks
Adds first-class support for long-running work. Instead of a tool call blocking until completion (or a client inventing its own polling convention), the Tasks extension gives MCP a standard way to kick off work, check status, and retrieve a result later — useful for anything that takes longer than a typical request timeout (large builds, batch data jobs, multi-step agent workflows).

---

## Authorization Hardening

The new spec aligns MCP's authorization flow more closely with standard OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect deployments, closing gaps that had made enterprise identity-provider integration awkward. Alongside this, the **Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA)** extension — previously experimental — was promoted to stable status.

EMA gives organizations a centralized way to control which MCP servers their users can reach, enforced through the org's existing identity provider. The goal is to replace today's per-server consent prompts ("allow this server to access X?", repeated for every server a user connects to) with a zero-touch flow: a user signs in once, and access to org-approved servers just works without further per-server setup.

---

## Formal Deprecation Policy

The spec also adopts a formal policy for deprecating and removing protocol features going forward — a sign of MCP's maturity as older stopgap mechanisms (some early transport and session-handling behavior) get phased out in favor of the stateless core.

---

## Ecosystem Scale

By March 2026, MCP SDK downloads reached roughly **97 million per month**, up from about 2 million at launch in November 2024 — a rough 50x increase in under a year and a half. That growth is a big part of why this revision focuses on production concerns (load balancing, enterprise auth) rather than new tool-calling primitives: the protocol's core interaction model was already proven, and the gaps were operational.

---

## Why It Matters

- **For server authors:** you can drop custom session-affinity logic and run behind a plain load balancer once clients and servers adopt the stateless core.
- **For enterprises:** EMA removes the "click allow" friction multiplied across every MCP server an org adopts, replacing it with identity-provider-gated access.
- **For UI-heavy tools:** MCP Apps standardizes what had been ad hoc — servers returning raw HTML or asking hosts to special-case rendering — into a reviewable, sandboxed mechanism.
- **For long-running agents:** Tasks removes the need for every server to reinvent polling for slow operations.
